items.title: L7: Choosing which example to use
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles guidance; Civil Service Jobs interview guidance
items.body: When you have a bank of examples, the skill is matching the right one to each question. Start with the verb and the context in the question. 'Tell us about a time you persuaded someone' points to Communicating and Influencing, and needs a story where someone started by disagreeing or being unsure. Next, check the example is recent enough to be credible, usually within the last two or three years, although an older example can be fine if nothing recent fits and you explain why. Check it is at the right level: an example that shows you following clear instructions is weaker at EO than one where you decided how to approach a problem. Check that it has a real result you can describe. Where two examples fit, prefer the one that lets you give more detail about your own actions. Avoid using the same example for two behaviours in one interview unless you have no choice; panels notice repeated stories and it narrows the evidence they have about you. If you must reuse a story, emphasise a different part of it, for instance the persuading in one answer and the planning in another. Examples can come from work, study, volunteering, caring or community roles, provided they show the behaviour. Finally, never stretch a good story to fit a poor match. If the fit is weak, say a short sentence acknowledging the angle you will take, and answer with the behaviour in the question at the centre.

questions.prompt: The question starts 'Tell us about a time you persuaded someone'. Which example fits best?

options.text: Following a manager's step-by-step instructions to update a record accurately
Attending a training course on communication skills and passing the assessment
Working alone to finish a report well ahead of the deadline
Convincing a reluctant colleague to try a new filing method

questions.hint: The story needs someone who started unsure or disagreeing.

questions.prompt: Which feature makes an example less credible?

options.text: It happened a very long time ago and nothing recent fits
It involved working closely with only one other person on the task
It took place in a voluntary role rather than paid employment
It produced a modest result rather than a dramatic one

questions.hint: Recency affects credibility, though an older story can be explained.

questions.prompt: At EO level, which example is likely to be stronger?

options.text: You were told which records to copy into a spreadsheet and did so accurately
You chose how to tackle a messy filing backlog and agreed it with your manager
You attended the team meeting regularly and took the minutes for your manager
You followed a clear checklist set out by your supervisor and completed every step

questions.hint: EO examples show more independence in how work is done.

questions.prompt: Two examples fit a question equally well. Which should you choose?

options.text: The one that happened most recently, even if it matches the behaviour less closely
The one you already used on your application form, so the panel sees consistency
The one that lets you give more detail about your own actions
The one that involved the more senior people, because it shows you work at a higher level

questions.hint: Action detail is what is scored.

questions.prompt: Why should you avoid using the same example for two behaviours in one interview?

options.text: It makes your answers noticeably longer than the time the panel has set aside
It narrows the evidence the panel has about you
It suggests you have a poor memory of what you have done at work
It breaks the interview rules, and the panel may stop the interview if you do it

questions.hint: Variety gives the panel more to score.

questions.prompt: You must reuse a story. What is the best way to handle it?

options.text: Add detail to the result in the second telling to make it fit better
Apologise and ask the panel whether you may skip the second question
Emphasise a different part of the story for each behaviour
Tell it identically each time so the panel can see you are consistent

questions.hint: Different angles bring out different behaviours.

questions.prompt: Where can examples come from?

options.text: Only roles that were held at the same grade as the one applied for
Only posts held previously within the Civil Service itself
Only paid work done in an office environment in the last twelve months
Work, study, volunteering, caring or community roles that show the behaviour

questions.hint: Any real setting can show the behaviour.

questions.prompt: No example fits a question well. What is the sound approach?

options.text: Briefly say the angle you will take and keep the question's behaviour at the centre
Describe what you would do in such a situation, instead of a real example
Use your best story as it stands and let the panel decide how it fits
Explain that you have no relevant experience and ask to move on

questions.hint: Keep the behaviour in the question central.

questions.prompt: Which question wording is the clearest signal that a story should involve disagreement?

options.text: 'Tell us about a time you had to change someone's mind.'
'Tell us about a time you worked as part of a team.'
'Tell us about a time you had to learn something new quickly.'
'Tell us about a time you had to meet a tight deadline.'

questions.hint: Changing a mind implies an initial difference of view.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the weakest reason for choosing an example?

options.text: It lets you explain your own actions in detail
It matches the behaviour asked and has a clear result you can describe
It is recent and shows decisions you made yourself
It is the story you feel most comfortable telling, whatever the question

items.title: L7: Making Effective Decisions in practice
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Behaviours (Making Effective Decisions); Civil Service Code
items.body: Making Effective Decisions is about using evidence, weighing options and being clear about the reasoning. At entry level, the indicators usually involve following procedures, asking when unsure and using information correctly. At EO level they move towards gathering information from a few sources, weighing up simple options and explaining your decision to others. At higher grades the behaviour widens to include risk, ambiguity and the wider consequences of choices. A strong answer therefore has a visible sequence: what the decision was, what information you collected, which options you considered, why you chose one, and what happened. Panels often probe with 'What other options did you consider?' or 'What would have changed your mind?'. Good candidates can answer, showing they weighed things up rather than guessed. A decision is not made worse by being cautious: knowing when to escalate is itself good judgement. For example, deciding to check a doubtful case with a senior colleague before approving a payment shows awareness of limits. The Civil Service Code's objectivity value means decisions should rest on evidence, not personal preference or pressure from others. A common weakness is describing a decision that was really an instruction followed, or one made on gut feeling with no reasoning. Another is explaining the outcome only, without the thinking that produced it. Strong answers also admit what was uncertain and how the candidate coped with it.

questions.prompt: Which answer best shows Making Effective Decisions at EO level?

options.text: Working through the backlog in the order your manager listed it, as instructed
Comparing two ways to clear a backlog, choosing one and explaining why to the team
Picking the option that looked quickest and starting straight away
Asking a more experienced colleague which approach to use and following their choice

questions.hint: The behaviour is about weighing options and explaining reasoning.

questions.prompt: A panel asks 'What other options did you consider?' What is it testing?

options.text: Whether you can remember the dates and sequence of what happened
Whether your manager agreed with the option you picked
Whether you weighed alternatives or just guessed
Whether you prefer working on your own or with others

questions.hint: Probes look for visible weighing up.

questions.prompt: A candidate checks a doubtful case with a senior colleague before approving a payment. How is this seen?

options.text: As a sign that the candidate had not read the guidance properly
As unnecessary delay for a payment the candidate could have approved
As good judgement about the limits of their authority
As a lack of decisiveness that slowed the work down

questions.hint: Escalating appropriately is a sign of sound judgement.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best describes a strong decision answer?

options.text: Outcome first, then the decision, then who agreed with it
Decision, information gathered, options, choice and reasons, outcome
The problem, how you felt about it, then what your manager decided
Instructions received, task completed, then thanks from the manager

questions.hint: A visible sequence shows the thinking.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the weakest evidence of Making Effective Decisions?

options.text: 'I went with my gut, and it turned out fine.'
'I checked three previous cases before replying.'
'I listed the risks and chose the lowest.'
'I asked the policy team a question and then chose.'

questions.hint: Gut feeling without reasoning is not evidence of a decision process.

questions.prompt: What does the Code's objectivity value mean for decisions?

options.text: Decisions should always be approved by a manager before they are acted on
Decisions should follow the view of the majority in the team
Decisions should be made as quickly as the situation allows
They should rest on evidence, not preference or pressure

questions.hint: Objectivity is about evidence-based advice and decisions.

questions.prompt: A candidate describes following a manager's step-by-step instructions exactly. What is the problem for a decision question?

options.text: It is an instruction followed, not a decision made
It shows too much initiative for the grade being recruited
It shows excessive caution about acting without being told
It shows a lack of respect for the manager who gave the instructions

questions.hint: The question asks for the candidate's own judgement.

questions.prompt: Which is the best response to 'What would have changed your mind?'

options.text: Say that you would have asked your manager what to do instead
Say that nothing could have changed your mind, as the decision was clearly right
Say that you have no idea, since decisions are made in the moment
Name the specific evidence that would have led to a different choice

questions.hint: Shows the decision was based on criteria.

questions.prompt: Why is it useful to admit uncertainty in a decision story?

options.text: It avoids follow-up questions about the parts you were unsure of
It shows you can act sensibly when information is incomplete
It allows you to skip describing the result of the decision
It makes the answer shorter so there is more time for other questions

questions.hint: Handling uncertainty is part of the behaviour at higher grades.

questions.prompt: A candidate explains only the outcome of a decision. What is missing?

options.text: The exact date on which the decision was made
The name of the manager who approved the decision
The thinking that led to the choice
The size and grade of the team affected

questions.hint: Reasoning is what the panel scores.

items.title: L7: Same behaviour, different grades
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Behaviours; Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body: The same behaviour is assessed differently depending on the grade of the job. The Civil Service publishes behaviour descriptors for each level, from Administrative Assistant and Administrative Officer, through Executive Officer, Higher and Senior Executive Officer, to Grade 7 and Grade 6, and the Senior Civil Service. As the grade rises, the expectations shift in three ways. First, scope: the examples move from your own tasks, to a small process, then to a team, a service or a wider system. Second, independence: lower grades follow clear guidance and ask when unsure, while higher grades decide how to proceed, handle ambiguity and challenge. Third, influence: higher grades are expected to shape what others do, build relationships across organisations and balance competing demands. Take Communicating and Influencing. At AO you might show clear, polite writing and speaking and checking people understand. At EO you might show adapting your style to different audiences and influencing a colleague. At HEO and SEO you might be expected to persuade senior people or external stakeholders, handle difficult messages and explain reasons. A candidate who offers an AO-level story for an HEO post is likely to score lower even if the story is excellent. The reverse is not a problem: a strong example above grade can be fine, provided you explain your actual role and do not overstate it. Always read the advert, which states the grade and the behaviours, and compare your examples with the descriptors for that grade.

questions.prompt: Which three shifts generally mark higher-grade expectations?

options.text: Longer hours, more meetings and bigger teams
Greater speed, more detail and less discussion
More technical skill, less contact with others and fewer decisions
Wider scope, more independence and greater influence

questions.hint: The descriptors broaden in scope, independence and influence.

questions.prompt: A candidate applying for an HEO role gives an excellent example of following an instruction accurately. How is it likely to score?

options.text: Lower than the role requires, because it is pitched at AO level
Highest of all, because simple tasks are described most clearly
The same as any other example, as the panel does not look at grade
Very high, because accuracy matters most at every grade

questions.hint: The example must meet the grade's descriptors.

questions.prompt: Which Communicating and Influencing example best fits EO level?

options.text: Briefing a Permanent Secretary on a complex policy decision and its risks
Adjusting how you explain a change to two different audiences and persuading a colleague to adopt it
Writing a clear, polite email to a customer exactly as your manager instructed
Typing up the notes of a meeting and circulating them to the attendees

questions.hint: EO adds adapting style and some influence.

questions.prompt: An example drawn from above your grade can be fine. What must you do?

options.text: Choose a different question so that the example is not needed
Avoid saying what you personally did, so the grade is not an issue
Explain your actual role clearly and not overstate it
Claim the senior role as your own, since you worked closely with it

questions.prompt: Where do you find the behaviours and grade for a job?

options.text: From the department's social media posts about its work
From the scores given to earlier candidates for similar posts
From a friend who already works in the department and knows the role
In the job advert and the published descriptors for the grade

questions.hint: The advert states the grade and the behaviours.

questions.prompt: Which is the clearest sign of increasing scope as grades rise?

options.text: Examples become longer and use more technical language as the grade rises
Examples move from your own tasks to a team, a service or a wider system
Examples include more email and written correspondence at higher grades
Examples are drawn from a longer period of employment at each higher grade

questions.prompt: How does independence usually differ between AO and HEO?

options.text: AO follows clear guidance and asks when unsure, while HEO decides how to proceed in ambiguous cases
AO is expected to set strategy for the team, while HEO follows the direction given
AO usually works mostly alone, while HEO is expected to work closely with others
AO takes more risks in the way work is done, while HEO is expected to avoid risk

questions.prompt: A candidate for an EO role describes advising a minister's private office. What might the panel think?

options.text: That the answer is clear and needs no questions to test it
That the candidate is unsuitable for the grade and the answer should stop
It may be above grade, so they will probe the candidate's actual role
That the answer is irrelevant and will be ignored for scoring

questions.hint: Panels check the real level of responsibility.

questions.prompt: Which is the most useful comparison before an interview?

options.text: Your examples against those you heard another candidate use in a mock interview
Your examples against the descriptors for the grade you are applying for
Your examples against your current job description and nothing else
Your examples against the descriptors for the grade above the one advertised

questions.prompt: Which wording would signal HEO-level influence?

options.text: 'I reminded a colleague about a deadline that we were both working towards.'
'I passed on a message from my manager to the rest of the team.'
'I persuaded a senior stakeholder to change timelines by setting out the risks.'
'I filed the minutes of the weekly meeting in the shared folder.'

questions.hint: Persuading senior people with reasons is higher-grade.

items.title: L7: Answering when you lack direct experience
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Many applicants for EO roles are early in their career or changing field. Panels know this and the behaviours are designed to be shown in many settings. Transferable examples are valid when the behaviour is real. A shift supervisor at a supermarket, a carer for a relative, a student running a society, a volunteer with a local charity, and a parent organising a school event can all show planning, working with others and managing a quality service. What counts is what you did, why, and what changed. If a question asks about a situation you have not met, such as handling a complaint from a member of the public, choose the closest real parallel, for instance dealing with an upset customer or a confused student, and say briefly how it is similar. Do not invent experience. Panels will probe, and false claims breach the Civil Service Code's honesty value. If you are asked about technical knowledge you lack, say so plainly, explain what you do know and how you would find out. That shows learning ability, and the Success Profiles value potential as well as current experience. Another approach is to demonstrate preparation: describe what you have read or done to learn about the role. For gaps in work history, state the reason briefly and neutrally, mention what you did during the gap, if relevant, and move to what you can offer. There is no need to over-apologise. Confidence comes from knowing your examples well, not from claiming more than you have.

questions.prompt: An applicant has never worked in an office. What type of example is valid?

options.text: Only paid work done within an office environment during the last two years
Only study at a university or college, since it is formally assessed
Only previous posts held within government or the wider public sector
Any real example showing the behaviour, such as volunteering or organising an event

questions.hint: Behaviours can be shown in many settings.

questions.prompt: What counts most in a transferable example?

options.text: What you did, why, and what changed
The job title you held at the time of the example
The size and reputation of the organisation you worked in
How impressive the setting sounds to the panel

questions.prompt: You are asked about handling a complaint from a member of the public, but you have not done this. What is a sensible approach?

options.text: Invent a complaint case that closely matches the question
Choose the closest real parallel and say how it is similar
Describe what you have read about how complaints are handled
Say you cannot answer because you lack that experience

questions.hint: A real parallel is honest and relevant.

questions.prompt: Why should you not invent experience?

options.text: It lowers your confidence, which then shows in later answers
It only matters in senior roles, where honesty is tested more closely
Panels dislike long answers and invented stories tend to be long
Panels probe, and false claims breach the honesty value of the Code

questions.prompt: You are asked about a technical tool you have never used. What is the best response?

options.text: Say you have not used it and then move on without saying more
Say you have used it, then move to a related tool you know better
Say plainly you haven't used it, explain related knowledge and how you would learn
Say it is unlikely to be needed in the role so the panel need not ask

questions.hint: Honesty plus learning ability scores better than bluff.

questions.prompt: Which Success Profiles idea supports a candidate with limited experience?

options.text: That potential is assessed as well as current experience
That only past experience is assessed, so potential is not scored
That grades are fixed by a candidate's age and length of service
That ability tests replace the need for any interview

questions.hint: Potential is part of the assessment.

questions.prompt: How should a gap in work history usually be handled?

options.text: Give a brief, neutral reason, mention anything relevant you did, then move to what you can offer
Give a long and detailed account of the reasons, covering every month of it
Say that your personal circumstances are not a matter for the panel to ask about
Avoid mentioning it unless the panel raises it directly, and then answer briefly

questions.prompt: Which statement best shows preparation when you lack direct experience?

options.text: 'I am a fast learner and I am sure I will pick the role up quickly.'
'I have always wanted to work in this department and I admire its work.'
'I have read the department's published guidance and spoken to someone who does this work.'
'I think this is a role in which I could do well and grow over time.'

questions.prompt: A candidate over-apologises for lack of experience. What is the effect?

options.text: It shows humility, which panels reward
It draws attention to the gap and weakens confidence
It prevents the panel from asking further questions
It earns extra marks for honesty

questions.prompt: Which of these is a real, transferable example for Managing a Quality Service?

options.text: Listing your qualifications at the start of your answer to the panel
Reading about quality standards on a public website and noting the main points
Watching a colleague answer queries from members and learning from them
Checking and improving how a volunteer rota was shared with members

questions.hint: A real action shows the behaviour.

items.title: L7: Conflict and difficult colleague questions
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Working Together; Civil Service Code
items.body: Panels often ask about disagreement or working with someone difficult. They are not looking for a story with a villain. They want to see maturity: how you handled the situation, protected the work and kept relationships. A strong answer usually follows this path. You noticed the problem early, spoke to the person directly and privately, listened to their view, and focused on the issue rather than the person. You looked for common ground, such as a shared goal, and agreed a way forward. If that did not work, you involved your manager, with facts rather than complaints. A weaker answer blames the other person, goes straight to the manager, or avoids the problem until it grows. Be careful about confidentiality and fairness: do not speak badly of named colleagues or reveal personal details. You can describe someone's behaviour factually, such as 'they often missed deadlines', without criticising their character. In the Code's terms, treating others with respect is part of integrity and impartiality. If the disagreement was about a decision, show that you stated your view, listened, and then supported the decision once made, even if it went against you. This is a sign of Working Together. Strong candidates also describe the learning: for example, agreeing expectations earlier in future. If the answer involves bullying or harassment, reporting through proper channels is appropriate, and the panel will expect that.

questions.prompt: What are panels mainly looking for in a conflict answer?

options.text: A clear villain and hero in the story, so that the panel can see who was right
Maturity in handling the situation, protecting the work and keeping relationships
A dramatic moment as the high point of the story, to hold the panel's interest
Proof that you won the argument in the end and that your view was adopted

questions.hint: The aim is to see how you behave.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest first step in a disagreement with a colleague?

options.text: Speaking to them directly and privately and listening to their view
Ignoring the problem for a while in case it passes
Copying the team into an email setting out your complaint
Telling your manager straight away, before speaking to the colleague

questions.prompt: When is involving your manager appropriate in a conflict story?

options.text: Only once the colleague has left the team
As the very first step in every case, so that the problem is on record
Never, because involving a manager shows weakness
When direct discussion has not worked, with facts rather than complaints

questions.hint: Escalation comes after trying to resolve it.

questions.prompt: Which description of a difficult colleague is best?

options.text: 'They do not care about the team or the standard of what we deliver.'
'They are simply impossible to work with, whatever you try with them.'
'They often missed deadlines, which affected my work.'
'They are lazy and unreliable and it showed in the work they produced.'

questions.prompt: A decision goes against your view. What shows Working Together?

options.text: Withdrawing your effort on the work until the decision is looked at again
Quietly working in a way that avoids following the decision in practice
Continuing to argue your case after the decision has been made and recorded
Stating your view, listening, then supporting the decision once made

questions.prompt: Which value in the Civil Service Code relates to treating colleagues with respect and fairness?

options.text: Integrity and impartiality
Ambition and loyalty
Speed and efficiency
Independence and secrecy

questions.hint: Fair and respectful behaviour is part of the values.

questions.prompt: What should you do in an answer when the situation involved bullying?

options.text: Leaving it out of the answer altogether
Dealing with it entirely on your own without telling anyone
Show you reported it through proper channels
Confronting the person publicly in front of the team

questions.hint: Reporting through the proper route is correct.

questions.prompt: A candidate finishes a conflict story without any learning. What is missing?

options.text: The names of everyone involved in the disagreement
Reflection on what they would do differently or have changed
A longer description of the office and the setting
An apology to the other person, included in the story

questions.hint: Learning is part of a strong answer.

questions.prompt: Why is it unwise to name a colleague and criticise them in an answer?

options.text: It breaks the STAR structure the panel expects
It can breach confidentiality and fairness, and reflects badly on you
Panels never ask about colleagues, so it would be irrelevant
It lengthens the answer beyond what can be scored

questions.prompt: Which wording best shows a focus on the issue rather than the person?

options.text: 'They never accepted that I was right about how the report should be done.'
'They refused to listen to anything I suggested about the deadline.'
'They were obstructive about the whole piece of work from the start.'
'We both wanted the report on time, so I suggested splitting the sections.'

items.title: L7: Pressure, priorities and competing demands
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Delivering at Pace; Managing a Quality Service
items.body: Questions about pressure test whether you can stay organised and keep quality when demands rise. Panels listen for method, not just for hard work. A strong answer shows how you prioritised: you listed the tasks, checked deadlines and impact, agreed priorities with your manager where needed, and communicated what could slip. 'Urgent' and 'important' are different: a task due today may be less valuable than one that affects many people next week. Good candidates explain the trade-off they made and why. They also show they kept checking quality, for instance by building in a final review of high-risk work, rather than rushing. A common weakness is a story of working extra hours, with no planning; this shows effort but not skill, and may suggest an unsustainable approach. Another is saying yes to everything. Strong answers include saying no or negotiating: 'I explained I could deliver one by Wednesday and the other by Friday, and asked which mattered most.' This shows honesty with stakeholders. The Success Profiles also expect people to look after their own wellbeing and to ask for support when workloads are unrealistic. Mentioning that you raised an unmanageable workload early is a positive sign, not a weakness. Finally, show what you learned, such as starting a task tracker or checking priorities every Monday, which demonstrates continuous improvement.

questions.prompt: Which element do panels mainly look for in a pressure answer?

options.text: How tired the pressure left you
How many tasks you completed in total
A method for prioritising, not just hard work
The number of hours you worked

questions.hint: Method matters more than effort alone.

questions.prompt: Which task is usually higher priority?

options.text: An important task affecting many people next week, even if another is due today
Whichever task a colleague asked about first, as a matter of courtesy
Whichever task is easiest to finish quickly so that the list gets shorter
Whichever task is due soonest, whatever its effect on others later on

questions.prompt: A candidate says 'I worked late every night and got it all done.' What is the weakness?

options.text: It shows poor timekeeping at the start of each day
It is too short to be a good example of anything
It shows effort but little skill in planning or prioritising
It shows too much honesty about how the work was done

questions.prompt: Which statement shows a good approach to competing demands?

options.text: 'I explained I could deliver one by Wednesday and the other by Friday, and asked which mattered most.'
'I let my manager decide what to do about both, as it was their call.'
'I said yes to both requests and worked late to fit them both in.'
'I did the easier one first, as it was quicker, and then began the other.'

questions.prompt: Why is raising an unmanageable workload early viewed positively?

options.text: It avoids the need to take on any future work
It makes the answer longer and so easier to score
It shows that the candidate cannot cope with normal work
It shows honesty, planning and attention to quality and wellbeing

questions.prompt: How might a candidate show quality was protected under pressure?

options.text: Doing the work in a different order each day
Building in a final review for high-risk work
Handing the work over without comment so others can check it
Skipping checks on lower-risk work to save time

questions.hint: Quality checks are part of the method.

questions.prompt: Which is a sign of continuous improvement after a busy period?

options.text: Taking a short holiday after the busy period
Asking to change line manager
Starting a task tracker or weekly priority check
Moving desks to be closer to the team

questions.prompt: Which behaviour does a question on prioritising workload mainly test?

options.text: Seeing the Big Picture
Leadership
Developing Self and Others
Delivering at Pace

questions.hint: Managing workload and deadlines is Delivering at Pace.

questions.prompt: What is a weakness in saying yes to every request?

options.text: You may not deliver any of them to the required quality
It shows you are flexible, which is the only point that matters
It shows you are well prepared for any task
It annoys the panel, who prefer candidates to refuse work

questions.prompt: Why should a pressure answer mention who you communicated with?

options.text: It makes the answer sound more senior than the role you held
Telling people what might slip is part of managing expectations
Panels like to hear long lists of names to check the story
It avoids the need to describe the result of your work

items.title: L7: Situational dilemmas and the Civil Service Code
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code; GOV.UK
items.body: Some interviews include situational questions, which describe a dilemma and ask what you would do. The Civil Service Code is the best compass. Its four values are integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality. Integrity includes putting the obligations of public service above your own interests, managing public money properly and not accepting gifts or hospitality that might appear to influence you. Honesty means being truthful and not misleading others. Objectivity means basing advice on evidence. Impartiality means acting fairly and serving governments of any political persuasion. If you are asked to do something that conflicts with the Code, or you see something wrong, you can raise it with your line manager or your department's nominated officer. If you are not satisfied with the response, you can report it to the Civil Service Commission. Good answers to a dilemma follow a pattern: identify the issue, say which value applies, consider the options, choose the one consistent with the Code, and explain how you would act and who you would tell. Avoid dramatic leaps such as leaking to the press or quietly ignoring the problem. Equally, avoid answers that assume you need to solve everything alone. Where information is uncertain, say you would check facts first. Political activity, confidentiality of information, and personal relationships with suppliers are common themes. Assume the panel wants judgement, not the 'right' phrase from the Code.

questions.prompt: A supplier offers you a gift to thank you for your help. What is the best response in light of the Code?

options.text: Keep it, provided the supplier is not currently bidding for any of your work
Accept it, but do not mention it to anyone as it was freely offered to you
Accept it, as long as the gift is small and the supplier is a long-standing one
Decline politely, and report the offer if it is significant, as it could appear to influence you

questions.hint: Gifts that could appear to influence conflict with integrity.

questions.prompt: You see a colleague sharing confidential data with someone who should not receive it. What is a sound first action?

options.text: Report it through your manager or the nominated officer
Confront the colleague in front of others
Ignore it, as it is not part of your job
Post about what you saw on social media

questions.hint: The Code sets out proper routes for raising concerns.

questions.prompt: If you are not satisfied with how your concern was handled, what can you do under the Code?

options.text: Take no further action
Report it to the Civil Service Commission
Contact a newspaper to publicise the matter
Resign immediately from your post

questions.hint: The Commission is the route for unresolved concerns.

questions.prompt: Which value requires you to serve governments of any political persuasion?

options.text: Objectivity
Honesty
Impartiality
Integrity

questions.hint: Impartiality means acting fairly and serving any government.

questions.prompt: Which is the best first step in a dilemma answer?

options.text: Ask the panel which value they prefer
Pick the quickest option to resolve it
Identify the issue and the value that applies
Say you would do whatever your manager tells you

questions.hint: Start by framing the issue using the Code.

questions.prompt: Which response to uncertain information is most sensible?

options.text: Do nothing at all until someone else raises it
Say you would check the facts before acting
Act immediately on what you heard, to avoid delay
Pass the information on to colleagues to see what they think

questions.prompt: A dilemma answer says you would leak the matter to the press. How would a panel view it?

options.text: As a leap that ignores proper routes
As admirably decisive
As irrelevant
As the correct application of the Code

questions.prompt: Which of these shows integrity?

options.text: Getting the work done by whatever means are quickest, whoever is affected

options.text: Giving the answer your manager is known to prefer

items.title: L7: Spotting problems in a strengths answer
items.source: Civil Service Jobs strengths-based interview guidance; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Strengths-based interviews use shorter, quicker questions and do not require a past example. That makes them harder to rehearse and easier to answer badly when you try to fit them to a template. Watch for several common problems. The first is the over-long answer: speaking for two or three minutes on a question meant to take under a minute, which loses energy. The second is the generic answer: 'I like helping people' without saying how or why. The third is the mismatch: choosing what you think the panel wants rather than what is true, which usually shows because your energy drops or your later answers contradict it. The fourth is overuse of a strength. A strength such as attention to detail can become a weakness if it leads to missing deadlines, and the best candidates acknowledge this: 'I enjoy getting details right, so I make sure I set a time limit to avoid over-checking'. This shows self-awareness. The fifth is dismissing a weakness question: strengths interviews usually include questions about what you find hard or what drains you. A good answer names something real but manageable and says how you cope. Examples include finding it tiring to work without any contact with others, or finding it hard to leave a task unfinished. Do not choose a fake weakness. Strengths interviews also reward warmth, curiosity and a willingness to learn. Finally, avoid asking for time to think too often; a short pause is fine, but repeated delays break the pace of the interview.

questions.prompt: A candidate speaks for three minutes on a strengths question. What is the likely problem?

options.text: It is the length panels normally expect
The answer is too long for the format and loses energy
It shows too much knowledge of the role
It makes the answer more convincing by adding detail

questions.prompt: 'I like helping people.' What is missing?

options.text: How and why, ideally with a small example
A full STAR structure
A longer description of the role you hold
A reference to the job advert

questions.prompt: A candidate says they love detail, then in another answer says they dislike checking work. What does the panel notice?

options.text: A sign of flexibility
Nothing, as questions are separate
Perfect consistency
A mismatch worth exploring

questions.prompt: Which answer shows self-awareness about a strength overused?

options.text: 'I enjoy getting details right, so I set a time limit to avoid over-checking.'
'I check everything repeatedly until I am sure that it is entirely right.'
'I am a perfectionist, so I sometimes find it hard to stop checking.'
'I never make mistakes in my work, so my attention to detail is a strength.'

questions.hint: Acknowledging the cost and how you manage it.

questions.prompt: Which is a good answer to 'What drains you?'

options.text: 'Nothing really drains me, because I enjoy every part of my work.'
'Colleagues who do not work as hard as I do, which I find frustrating.'
'I find it tiring to work with no contact with others, so I arrange regular catch-ups.'
'Doing any kind of work at all, if I am honest about how I feel.'

questions.hint: A real but manageable weakness with a coping approach.

questions.prompt: Why is a fake weakness a poor choice?

options.text: It shortens the answer too much to be scored
It sounds rehearsed and undermines honesty
It prevents the panel from asking follow-up questions
It conflicts with the Civil Service Code

questions.prompt: What can the panel see when a candidate says what they think the panel wants?

options.text: A perfectly matched profile
A shorter interview
A high score for matching the role
A drop in energy and later contradictions

questions.prompt: How often can you pause to think in a strengths interview?

options.text: As long as you need each time, without limit

questions.prompt: Which trait do strengths interviews tend to reward?

options.text: Warmth, curiosity and willingness to learn

Long, detailed speeches that cover the whole of a topic
Technical vocabulary that shows knowledge of the role

questions.prompt: Why do panels use short, quick questions in strengths interviews?

options.text: They are easier to score

items.title: L7: Probing and follow-up questions in practice
items.source: Civil Service Jobs interview guidance; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Follow-up questions are normal in structured interviews. They are used to fill gaps in the evidence so that scoring is fair. The panel may use the same prompts with every candidate, such as 'What was your role?', 'What did you say?', 'What was the result?' or 'What would you do differently?'. Learn to read what a probe is asking for. 'What exactly did you say?' wants the words, not a summary. 'Why did you choose that?' wants your reasoning. 'What happened next?' wants the outcome. 'How did you know it worked?' wants evidence. 'What would you do differently?' wants reflection and learning. When you hear a probe, answer it directly and then stop. Common errors are repeating the original answer, or becoming defensive. A probe is not criticism; it is the panel completing its notes. If you do not have the detail, say so honestly rather than inventing it: 'I don't remember the exact figure, but it was roughly...'. If you realise your example does not fit the probe, say that and offer the part that does. If you are asked several probes in a row, it may mean the panel is close to a score and is checking one box. Stay calm. Avoid saying 'as I said before'. Instead, give a short, fresh answer. If a probe makes you realise a weakness in the example, you can acknowledge it, and say what you learned. That often scores well, because it shows honesty.

questions.prompt: What is the panel usually trying to do with a follow-up question?

options.text: Signal that the answer was wrong
Shorten the interview
Fill gaps in the evidence so scoring is fair
Catch the candidate out

questions.prompt: 'What exactly did you say?' What does the panel want?

options.text: A general description of the conversation
The words you used, not a summary
The words the other person used
Your feelings at the time

questions.prompt: 'How did you know it worked?' What is the panel asking for?

options.text: Evidence of the outcome
Your own opinion about the outcome
A repeat of the action you took
Your manager's name

questions.prompt: 'What would you do differently?' What is being tested?

options.text: Whether you remember the date
Whether you regret the work
Whether you blame others
Reflection and learning

questions.hint: Learning is part of the evidence.

questions.prompt: Which is a common error when answering a probe?

options.text: Repeating the original answer instead of giving the new detail
Answering the probe directly and then stopping
Giving a short fresh answer that adds the detail asked for
Admitting honestly that you do not remember a particular detail

questions.prompt: You do not remember a figure. What should you do?

options.text: Change the subject to another part of the story
Make up a figure that sounds plausible
Say there was no figure at all
Say you don't remember exactly and give an honest estimate

questions.prompt: Several probes follow in a row. What might this mean?

options.text: The panel is trying to trick you
The panel is checking one more point before scoring
The answer is failing and the panel is giving you a last chance

questions.prompt: Why avoid saying 'as I said before'?

options.text: It is rude to the panel, who may mark you down for it at once
It lowers the score automatically whenever a candidate repeats themselves
It can sound defensive; a short fresh answer is better
It breaks the interview rules, which require every answer to be new

questions.prompt: A probe reveals a weakness in your example. What is a good response?

options.text: Switch to a different example
Acknowledge it and say what you learned
Become defensive about the example
Deny it was a weakness

questions.hint: Honesty about limits often scores well.

questions.prompt: Your example does not fit a probe. What should you do?

options.text: Say so and offer the part of the example that does fit
Invent a connection to the question
Repeat the original story from the start
Refuse to answer the probe

items.title: L7: Adjustments and fairness in realistic cases
items.source: Equality Act 2010; Civil Service Jobs guidance; Disability Confident scheme (GOV.UK)
items.body: The Equality Act 2010 protects people from discrimination and requires employers to make reasonable adjustments for disabled candidates. In Civil Service recruitment, adjustments are arranged through the recruitment team, usually by telling them in advance, ideally when you apply or accept the interview. Typical adjustments include extra time, rest breaks, written questions, a different format, accessible rooms, a British Sign Language interpreter, or breaks for medication. You do not have to share a full diagnosis; you explain what would help. Panels are trained to focus on the evidence and not to ask about health, family plans or other protected characteristics. Under the Act, employers are restricted from asking health questions before offering a job, except for limited reasons such as arranging adjustments. The Civil Service also uses the Disability Confident scheme, which in many competitions offers an interview to disabled applicants who meet the minimum criteria. If a panel member asks a question you feel is inappropriate, you can say politely that you would prefer not to answer, and bring your answer back to the role. Afterwards, you can raise concerns with the recruitment team or use the department's complaints process. Other fairness measures include structured questions, the same questions for all candidates, scoring against criteria and recording notes. Anonymised sifting may also be used in some competitions. If you believe an adjustment was not provided as agreed, tell the panel on the day or the recruitment team afterwards.

options.text: On the day, in the room, if the need arises
Once the interview is over
Only after an offer has been made
In advance, when applying or when accepting the interview

questions.hint: Early notice lets arrangements be made.

options.text: A guaranteed pass

questions.hint: Adjustments change how you are assessed, not the standard.

Just an explanation of what would help, rather than a full diagnosis

questions.hint: You explain needs, not necessarily diagnosis.

options.text: To limit the paperwork involved

items.title: L7: Presentations: structure, timing and questions
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; Civil Service Success Profiles: Communicating and Influencing
items.body: A presentation at interview usually tests whether you can organise information, communicate clearly and respond to challenge. Start with the answer or purpose, because busy readers and listeners want to know where you are going. A reliable structure is: say what the topic is and what you will recommend, give two or three reasons or points, address one risk or counter-argument, and end with a clear recommendation or next step. Use plain language and avoid jargon unless the audience uses it. Keep slides to a minimum, with one idea per slide and no dense text. If you have five minutes, plan for four and a half; run through it aloud with a timer. If you notice you are running over, drop the least important point rather than speaking faster. Do not read from slides: panels can read faster than you speak. Look at the panel, not the screen. In the question session, listen to the whole question, pause, and answer directly. If you do not know, say what you would do to find out. If a question challenges your recommendation, acknowledge the point, explain your reasoning and say what would change your view; this shows judgement and openness. If a technical problem prevents your slides appearing, continue without them, using your notes. Panels judge the message and delivery, not the software. Finally, be ready for the question, 'What would you do with more time or resources?', by naming a sensible next step.

questions.prompt: Where should the recommendation usually appear in a short presentation?

options.text: Never, as the panel should decide
At the start, then again at the end
Only at the very end
In the middle only

questions.prompt: What is a reliable presentation structure?

options.text: A list of facts in the order in which you happened to find them
A joke to relax the panel, a story to engage them, then a quotation

options.text: Plan for ten minutes and cut it down on the day

options.text: It breaks the interview rules, which forbid the use of visual aids

options.text: Defend your position more firmly, repeating the strongest reason you gave earlier
Acknowledge the point, explain your reasoning and say what would change your view

options.text: Continue without them using your notes
Cancel the presentation

options.text: Refuse to answer

options.text: Technical terms throughout, so the panel sees how expert you are

Long, carefully qualified sentences, so nothing is left out

options.text: An apology for what you left out
A request for a bigger budget

A sensible next step showing judgement

items.title: L7: Interpreting outcomes and feedback
items.source: Civil Service Jobs recruitment guidance; Civil Service Recruitment Principles
items.body: The outcome of a Civil Service interview is usually communicated by email or through the recruitment portal. You may be offered the job, placed on a reserve list, or told you were unsuccessful. Offers are conditional on pre-employment checks, references and, where needed, security clearance, so avoid resigning from your current job until you have confirmation that all conditions are met. Check the start date, grade, location and salary in writing. If you have another offer pending, you can ask for a short extension to make a decision, but there is no guarantee. Reserve lists last for a stated period and offers may come later, so reply promptly if contacted. Feedback is usually available by request, and it commonly lists your score for each behaviour, with comments. Interpret it carefully. A single low score may mean a weak example, not a weak candidate. Look for repeated comments, such as 'lacked detail on personal actions', which point to a fixable habit. Compare the feedback with your notes of what you said. Where feedback is general or unclear, you can ask the recruitment team for clarification. If you think scoring or process was unfair, you can ask the department to review it through its complaints procedure; the Civil Service Recruitment Principles require selection on merit through fair and open competition, and departments should be able to show their process. Finally, treat rejection as information, not a verdict. Many successful civil servants applied more than once.

options.text: Once you have confirmation that all conditions are met
